summary: Every yes/no answer in Still in View comes with its confidence and its evidence. The page tells a mission planner whether a lunar landing site still has sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth when a launch slips or the site changes. Confidence: each answer shows how far the Sun or Earth is above or below the horizon, and near the Moon's south pole, where the horizon is terrain, an answer that would change within one cell of NASA's LRO LOLA terrain grid (80 m) or with the lander's height is marked. Evidence: 972 of 972 random checks against NASA JPL Horizons give the same yes/no answer, with the Sun and Earth directions within 0.0105° on the sky; the terrain skyline matches NASA's PGDA illumination maps within 0.1 percentage points at IM-1 and IM-2 over the same 18.6 years; and one kilometre can decide: over one year at the IM-2 landing site, Earth's centre is above the skyline 80.1 % of the time, one kilometre east 64.4 %, one kilometre south 56.6 %. Each check can be repeated with one command. For planners: a GO / RISKY / NO-GO line with the longest night and an example battery size, a calendar of every site by day, ready comparisons such as "Launch slipped two weeks", lunar eclipses, a CSV of the hourly table, and dates to the end of 2070, at eighteen sites including six of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions, plus terrain for your own coordinates south of 75°S. Try it: https://aimanmalib.github.io/spaceapps26/

Try it: https://aimanmalib.github.io/spaceapps26/ (no sign-in). Code, Apache-2.0: https://github.com/aimanmalib/spaceapps26

IM-2 at 2026-11-06 20:00 UTC: Earth is 0.6° above the skyline, and the card marks the link answer as a close call: it changes inside the terrain range.

Confidence, then evidence

Every yes/no answer comes with both.

1. Confidence. Each answer shows how far the Sun or Earth is above or below the horizon used. Near the Moon's south pole the horizon is terrain, known only as well as the grid it was measured on: there the card marks an answer that would change within one LOLA cell (80 m) or with the lander's height.

2. Evidence. The angles agree with NASA JPL Horizons in 972 of 972 random checks: the same yes/no answer each time, and the Sun and Earth directions within 0.0105° on the sky. The terrain skyline is within 0.1 percentage points of NASA's own PGDA illumination maps at IM-1 and IM-2 over the same 18.6 years, with every place where it differs more shown and explained. And one kilometre can decide: over one year at the IM-2 site Earth's centre is above the skyline 80.1 % of the hours; one kilometre east, 64.4 %; one kilometre south, 56.6 %. Each check can be repeated with one command (README, "What a scientist can check").

For planners: a GO / RISKY / NO-GO line for each scenario with the longest night and an example battery size, a calendar of every site by day, ready comparisons such as "Launch slipped two weeks", eighteen sites with seven future south polar targets (six of NASA's nine Artemis III candidate regions), a terrain skyline for your own coordinates south of 75°S, lunar eclipses at the site, the hourly table behind each card as a CSV file, and dates to the end of 2070.

The view toward Earth from the IM-2 site at 2026-11-14 00:00 UTC, drawn to scale over the LOLA skyline. The buttons move the point 1 km north, east, south or west.

Impact: NASA reported that the IM-2 lander came down more than 400 meters from its intended site and that the mission ended less than a day after landing. When a landing date or site changes, this page gives the two answers the challenge asks about (sunlight for power, Earth in view for direct communication) for up to four scenarios side by side.

Creativity: the view toward Earth is drawn to scale over the terrain skyline, so a 1 km move that hides Earth shows in one picture. It also knows when Earth itself hides the Sun: lunar eclipses at the site, matched to NASA's eclipse list.

Validity: the Sun and Earth directions are within 0.0105° of JPL Horizons on the sky over 972 random checks; where the terrain horizon differs from NASA PGDA by more than 0.1 points, I show why (below).

Relevance: built from items in the challenge text: Sun and Earth visibility, side-by-side and sequential comparison, alternative future sites, rescheduling, custom coordinates, LOLA terrain and slopes, a lunar day and a year, an educational game.

NASA data: JPL Horizons, LRO LOLA, GSFC PGDA maps, the GSFC eclipse list, the JPL DSN handbook, NSSDCA, LROC, NASA Artemis III pages, NTRS papers.

What it does

- Pick a landing site: six Apollo landings, IM-1 (its nominal landing area and where it came to rest), IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4, seven future south polar targets, or your own latitude and longitude.

- The future targets are six of the nine Artemis III candidate landing regions NASA listed in October 2024 (Malapert Massif, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, Haworth, Mons Mouton Plateau, de Gerlache Rim 2) and the Shackleton connecting ridge, where NASA says Blue Moon Mark 1, a CLPS flight, will attempt a landing. Measured over the year: at the Malapert Massif point Earth's centre is above the skyline 34.3 % of the hours, 100.0 % one kilometre north and 0.0 % one kilometre south.

- Pick any UTC date and time from 2026-11-01 to the end of 2070. The first year comes from frozen JPL Horizons tables; later dates are computed in the browser, and each card says which.

- Read two answers: solar power possible or not, direct-to-Earth communication possible or not. Each comes with the elevation, the time left before sunset or Earthset, the window length, and whether the whole disc, part of it or none of it is above the horizon.

- Every card opens with one short verdict, for example "Link to Earth, no sunlight", and a 360° strip of the horizon with the Sun and Earth on it. At the ten south polar terrain sites the strip shows the LOLA skyline. On first load, the first card's strip plays one lunar day in 5 seconds, then stops on the chosen time.

- Try a comparison: ready-made comparisons above the cards: "Launch slipped two weeks", "IM-1: planned vs where it landed", "Apollo 11 vs the south pole", "Ridge: summer vs winter" and "Lunar eclipse at the south pole".

- Mission check on every card: a GO / RISKY / NO-GO line for a stay of 7, 14 or 29.5 days from the chosen time, with the share of hours with the Sun, Earth and both, the longest night, the longest gap without Earth, a geometry estimate in W/m², and an example battery size for the longest night (100 W load, in kWh); the GO limits are settings, not mission requirements. The card details also give the Moon's elevation from the three Deep Space Network complexes.

- Lunar eclipses at the site: when Earth passes in front of the Sun as seen from the site, the card says so. There is no sunlight for solar power while the Sun's centre is behind Earth, and the covered share lowers the power estimate. Example: IM-2 on 2027-08-17 at 07:00 UTC, the Sun is 6.3° above the LOLA skyline while Earth covers 54 % of it.

- Compare up to four scenarios as cards and in one side-by-side table.

- Step a card to the previous or next site, or one day earlier or later. "If the date moves" gives the same two answers for the next 14 days and counts the dates on which each one is possible.

- "Next windows" lists the next stretches, from the chosen time, when the Sun and Earth are both above the horizon without a break for at least 1, 3, 7 or 14 days, and a button moves the card to a window's start.

- "Copy link" puts the scenarios in a shareable web address, and "Set all to now (UTC)" moves every card to the current hour.

- Download CSV, at the foot of every card and under the side-by-side table: the hourly rows behind the mission check (UTC time, Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation, the horizon used, both answers, the source of the angles, and whether the Sun is behind Earth). It is made in the browser; nothing is sent.

- Take the tour: five steps for a first visit, from the decision to the Validation link, opened only by its button. Every page shares one header and footer.

- "Show me the one-kilometre example": one button that opens IM-2 at 2026-11-14 00:00 UTC and scrolls to the view toward Earth, where buttons move the point 1 km north, east, south or west.

- Play: a game of six rounds. For one site and time, answer the two questions; Check shows the real answers and margins, computed from the same data as the tool. Score out of 12.

- Teach: a 15-minute class activity in three steps (the game; Apollo 11 and IM-2 at the same time; the one-kilometre example), each with a question and a link to the tool.

- Overview: one table of all eighteen listed sites over the whole year (shares of hours in view, the longest stretch with both, the horizon used), sortable, and a calendar of every site by day: each cell splits that day's 24 hours into both in view, Sun only, Earth only and neither, and opens that day on Compare.

- At the ten south polar sites (IM-1 at two points, IM-2 and the seven future targets) the horizon is the terrain skyline from LRO LOLA, with a 2D map and a 3D surface of the ground 80 × 80 km around the site, and a view from the lander's own position with heights not stretched.

- Own coordinates south of 75°S get a terrain skyline too, computed in the browser from the LOLA grids (80 m near the pole, coarser elsewhere). Against the 80 m skylines of the ten listed terrain sites, both answers agree in 97.2 % to 99.9 % of the year's hours at nine sites and 93.4 % at the tenth, which the card names.

- Terrain range at the ten listed terrain sites: each card says whether an answer changes within the nine skylines 80 m apart around the site (observer at 0 m and 2 m). At IM-2 the Earth answer changes inside the range in 5.8 % of the year's hours.

- Buttons on the 2D map switch it to slope (computed from the same LOLA heights) or to NASA's average sunlight map (GSFC PGDA, share of time over 18.6 years with the Sun in view). The tool does not compute shadows on the map.

Two scenarios side by side: IM-2 at 2026-11-14 00:00 UTC and two days later; the Sun answer differs.

Why small shifts matter

NASA reported that the IM-2 lander came down on 6 March 2025 more than 400 meters from its intended site, inside a crater near the Moon's south pole. It was on its side, could not fully run its instruments before its batteries were depleted, and the mission ended less than a day after landing. This tool does not model that crater (its terrain grid is 80 m). It shows how little room there is at the south pole: one kilometre can decide whether Earth is in view.

At the IM-2 site on 2026-11-14 00:00 UTC, Earth is 1.3° above the terrain horizon. One kilometre east it is 1.5° below. One kilometre south it is 2.6° below. On an ideal sphere, one kilometre tilts the horizon by only 0.033°. Over a whole year of hourly steps, Earth's centre is above the skyline 80.1 % of the time at the site, 64.4 % one kilometre east and 56.6 % one kilometre south. Every card lists these shifts: 6 hours and 1 day either way, and 1 km north, east, south and west. Open this case: https://aimanmalib.github.io/spaceapps26/?s=im-2,2026-11-14T00:00

The button "Show me the one-kilometre example", then the view toward Earth from the site and from the points 1 km north, east, south and west (real screen capture).

LOLA heights around IM-2, with the terrain skyline and the directions of the Sun and Earth.

The same map with NASA's average sunlight layer (PGDA): 47 % at the IM-2 site, 0 % to 71 % on the map.

How it works

Python scripts ask JPL Horizons for the azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth at every site, one row per hour for one year. Other scripts trace the terrain skyline from the LOLA south polar elevation grids: one ray every 0.5° of azimuth, out to 300 km or the edge of the grid. The results are frozen as small JSON files; the page reads only those and calls no outside service. Own coordinates, and dates after 2027-11-01, are computed in the browser with Astronomy Engine on the same hourly grid; an own point south of 75°S gets its skyline in the browser from copies of the LOLA grids that ship with the site.

The IM-2 timeline over the whole year: Sun at least partly above the terrain horizon 45.7 % of the hours, Earth 93.2 %.

One year at every listed site. Most hours with both the Sun and Earth in view: Apollo 12 (Ocean of Storms), 49.6 %. Longest unbroken stretch with both: IM-2 Athena (Mons Mouton area), 15.8 days (2026-11-15 to 2026-11-30). Sites with a terrain skyline and sites on the ideal sphere use different horizons, so their numbers are not like for like.

Play: the first round after Check, Apollo 11 at 2026-11-20 00:00 UTC.

How I checked it

- Against JPL Horizons at scale: 720 random site-and-minute pairs, 40 at each of the eighteen sites from 2026-11-01 to 2030-12-31, on frozen-table and browser-computed dates: same power and communication answer in 720 of 720; largest angle difference 0.0152°, and on the sky at most 0.0061° for the Sun and 0.0063° for Earth. With the earlier checks (90 pairs on the frozen tables, 30 engine pairs at unnamed points, 132 pairs in 2028 to 2070): 972 pairs, every yes/no answer the same, directions within 0.0105° on the sky. The later-year check is judged on the sky: its largest azimuth difference, 0.1465° with the Sun 0.56° from the zenith, is 0.0015° there. The raw Horizons answers of the check at scale are kept in the repository.

- Terrain horizon against the NASA GSFC PGDA polar illumination maps, over the same 18.6 years: at IM-1 and IM-2 the share of time the Sun and Earth are visible differs by 0.1 percentage points or less; at the eight other listed terrain sites the Sun differs by 0.0 to 15.6 points, most at the Shackleton ridge point. At a check point 0.55° from the pole the Sun still differs by 17.6 points (85.3 % against NASA's 67.7 %). There the tool's value depends on detail smaller than one map pixel: 57.2 % with the observer on the ground, 85.3 % at 2 m (the height the tool uses). I report it as measured.

- At 100 random points south of 80°S (fixed seed), the same terrain check against PGDA with the one-year table: Sun median difference 0.9 percentage points (90th percentile 2.4, largest 10.7), Earth median 1.1 (90th percentile 5.6, largest 21.8).

- Lunar eclipses against NASA GSFC's eclipse list: from 2026-11-01 to 2031-01-01 the tables hold 142 stretches of hours with part of the Sun behind Earth at the eighteen sites, and every one lies within 2 hours of one of the 10 eclipses on NASA's list.

- Ground stations: at the time tested, the Moon's elevation from the three DSN complexes agrees with JPL Horizons within 0.001°.

- 348 automated tests (266 JavaScript, 82 Python) and browser smoke tests on desktop Chromium, a 320 px window and WebKit iPhone 13; the date field was also fixed after a test on a real iPhone. One command rebuilds the frozen tables, terrain data and checks from the NASA sources (docs/REPRODUCE.md).

The Validation page.

What it does not do

Every one-year number (Overview, calendar, year shares) covers the first year of dates only. The mission check is geometry only: its W/m² figure has no panel efficiency, its battery size uses an example load, and its GO limits are settings. The LOLA terrain horizon, the maps and the 1 km shifts exist only at the ten listed south polar sites; own coordinates south of 75°S get a skyline from coarser copies of the LOLA grids, with no map or 1 km shifts; every other site, and own coordinates north of 75°S, use the ideal sphere horizon. A future target is one point inside a candidate area, not a chosen landing point. The terrain range is a sensitivity range for the 80 m LOLA grid, not an error bar on the real ground. Answers are geometry only: no panel orientation, power output, antennas or link budgets; the ground-station line uses an example elevation limit. The interface is in English; Indonesian and Malay are optional SI translations, not reviewed by a native speaker.

Who it is for

One page for the three audiences the challenge names (mission planners, educators, the public): plain answers first, technical details one click away.

I hope that the next time a landing date slips, someone can open this page and see what changed: is there still sunlight, is Earth still in view. And I hope a teacher can use the one-kilometre example to show a class why the Moon's south pole is hard.

What I would do next follows from the limits above: bring the terrain horizon to any point south of 75°S instead of two sites, and add more years of dates.

Since that sentence was written, both have been started: own coordinates south of 75°S now get a LOLA skyline from a coarser grid, and dates run to the end of 2070. Still to do: the full 80 m grid at any point, and terrain finer than 80 m near the sites.

Tools

JavaScript (Vite 8, Astronomy Engine 2.1.19), Python 3 and NumPy, Node.js 22, Playwright for browser tests and screenshots. Code and data scripts were generated with Claude Code (Anthropic), an SI tool, under my direction. Generated files are labelled, and SI-DISCLOSURE.md in the repository says who decided what.

Other notes

Space agency partner data: none used.

Font: IBM Plex Sans (SIL Open Font License 1.1), served from the site itself. Images: real screenshots of this tool, plus one NASA photograph (Apollo 8, AS08-14-2383, credit: NASA).

Use of SI

I used Claude Code (Anthropic), a large language model coding tool.

Decided by me: to take part in the Jakarta event and this challenge; the three audiences and the twelve items to build, chosen from a list the SI drew from NASA's challenge text; the project name, from names the SI suggested; on 15 November, four further options from the challenge text and eight features the SI suggested, all chosen by me. On the evening of 15 November I set the aim of a Global Award, asked the SI to red-team the entry against it, and accepted these of its recommendations: changes from that review (the PGDA check over the same 18.6 years, the horizon strip with a verdict, the terrain range, more south polar sites), features that other public entries had and mine lacked (ready-made comparisons, the mission check, the calendar, the lander view, dates to 2030), and that night more additions it proposed (four more Artemis III regions, terrain for own coordinates, lunar eclipses with a battery estimate and ground stations, a visual pass with one header and footer, a JPL Horizons check at scale, a CSV download and a guided tour, an opening screen, dates to 2040 and 2050), at my request a first-load motion and dates to 2070, and my decision to judge the later-year check on directions on the sky.

Done by SI, on my instructions: a feasibility comparison of the challenges, the translation of the challenge text into Malay for me, the build order and the slide layout; the red-team review and its measurements, including the comparison with other public entries and their READMEs; the choice of sources for the added sites; all code, data scripts and tests; the checks and their numbers; the interface design and the visual pass; the optional Indonesian and Malay translations (not reviewed by a native speaker); and the English text of this form, the slides and the README, drafted from my choices and the measured results. Several SI sessions built features in parallel. Some feature ideas, and the confidence-then-evidence framing of this text, came from other public entries; no code, text or image was copied. The code, numbers and text added on the evening and night of 15 November are the SI's work on my instructions.

Not used: no SI-generated images, video or audio. The demo video is a screen recording of the site with scripted captions; no generated imagery or voice. Every image is a real screenshot of the tool, except one credited NASA photograph (Apollo 8, AS08-14-2383) on the home page, the About page and slide 1.

Where it is marked: generated source files carry the header "SI-generated: Claude Code (Anthropic)", data files a generated_by field in data/SOURCES.json, and each page an si-disclosure meta tag and a footer line. SI-DISCLOSURE.md gives the full statement.
